questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with sudden onset erythema and swelling of pre-existing skin lesions, along with painful nerve swelling. Fever is absent. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Stop MDT immediately and start systemic steroids
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction in borderline leprosy presents with acute inflammation of existing lesions and neuritis. Management is prednisolone (starting 40mg/day, tapered over 6 months) while continuing MDT unchanged. Thalidomide is reserved for Type 2 (ENL) reactions. MDT must never be stopped during reactions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has flaccid blisters on the trunk and painful oral erosions for 2 months. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis with basal cells remaining attached to the basement membrane ('tombstone' pattern). The most likely circulating autoantibody is against:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) targets desmoglein 3 (Dsg3), producing mucosal involvement. When both Dsg3 and Dsg1 antibodies are present, mucocutaneous disease occurs. Dsg1 alone causes pemphigus foliaceus (superficial, no mucosa). BP180 is the target in bullous pemphigoid. Transglutaminase antibodies are seen in dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child has patchy hair loss on the scalp. Wood's lamp examination reveals bright green fluorescence. KOH examination shows arthroconidia arranged around the outside of the hair shaft (ectothrix). The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis with characteristic bright green fluorescence on Wood's lamp (due to pteridine production). Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum cause endothrix infections (arthroconidia within the hair shaft) without fluorescence, presenting as 'black dot' ringworm. T. rubrum rarely causes tinea capitis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless, solitary ulcer on the glans penis with indurated, clean edges and a firm base for 10 days. Bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy is present. VDRL is non-reactive. The most appropriate next investigation is:
opts: Dark field microscopy of serous exudate
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, serological tests (VDRL, FTA-ABS, TPHA) may be non-reactive as they take 1-4 weeks after chancre appearance to become positive. Dark field microscopy of serous exudate from the chancre can directly demonstrate T. pallidum spirochetes and is the investigation of choice in the seronegative window period.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman has a photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, recurrent oral ulcers, and polyarthritis for 3 months. ANA is positive at 1:320. Which antibody would be MOST specific for confirming SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm antibodies are the MOST specific for SLE (~99% specificity), though they have low sensitivity (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is both specific (~95%) and sensitive for SLE, and titers correlate with disease activity. Anti-Ro/SSA occurs in SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, and neonatal lupus. Anti-histone antibodies are characteristic of drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 52-year-old diabetic man presents with 3 days of diffuse erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness of the lower leg following a minor cut. No abscess or bullae are present. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
questions.exp: Cellulitis in diabetic patients warrants IV antibiotics and requires coverage for both Group A Streptococcus and S. aureus. Cloxacillin is a beta-lactamase-stable penicillin effective against both organisms. Benzylpenicillin covers Streptococcus but not S. aureus. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for a diabetic patient with significant infection.

questions.q: A 68-year-old patient had herpes zoster affecting the right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve 4 months ago. The rash has fully healed but the patient reports continuous severe burning pain with allodynia in the same distribution. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is defined as pain persisting more than 3 months after resolution of the acute zoster rash. It is the most common complication of herpes zoster. Risk factors include age >60, severe acute pain, ophthalmic division involvement, and immunosuppression. Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves facial nerve (geniculate ganglion) causing ear pain, vesicles, and facial palsy.

questions.q: Excision biopsy of a pigmented lesion reveals malignant melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.8mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate <1/mm², no lymph node involvement, and no distant metastasis. Per AJCC 8th edition staging, the T category is:
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition melanoma T staging: T1 (<1.0mm), T2 (1.0-2.0mm), T3 (2.0-4.0mm), T4 (>4.0mm). Suffix 'a' = no ulceration; 'b' = with ulceration. At 1.8mm without ulceration = T2a. T3a would require thickness >2.0mm. T1b requires either ulceration or thickness 0.8-1.0mm.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy on dapsone develops pallor, jaundice, and dark urine 2 weeks into treatment. Hemoglobin is 7.5 g/dL. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. The most likely explanation is:
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent hemolysis in all patients, but severe hemolysis (with bite cells and Heinz bodies on smear) occurs in G6PD-deficient individuals who cannot regenerate NADPH to counter oxidative stress. G6PD screening before initiating dapsone is recommended. Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome presents as drug rash, fever, and lymphadenopathy 5-6 weeks after starting.

questions.q: Langerhans cells in the skin are best characterized as:
opts: Bone marrow-derived dendritic cells expressing CD1a and CD207 (Langerin), with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy
Neural crest-derived melanocyte precursors found in the basal layer
Resident tissue macrophages derived from circulating monocytes in the dermis
Mast cell progenitors found in the papillary dermis
questions.exp: Langerhans cells are bone marrow-derived antigen-presenting cells located in the suprabasal epidermis. They express CD1a and CD207 (Langerin). Birbeck granules (tennis racket-shaped organelles) on electron microscopy are pathognomonic. They capture antigens, migrate to regional lymph nodes, and present antigens to T cells, playing a central role in cutaneous immune surveillance.

questions.q: A 35-year-old hairdresser has chronic hand and face dermatitis. Patch testing shows +++ reaction to para-phenylenediamine (PPD) at D2 and D4. This patient is most likely to also react to which of the following?
questions.exp: PPD belongs to the para-amino group of chemicals that exhibit cross-reactivity. Benzocaine (para-aminobenzoate ester), sulfonamide antibiotics, thiazide diuretics, furosemide, PABA-containing sunscreens, and azo dyes all cross-react with PPD due to a shared para-amino benzene ring. Neomycin, lanolin, and nickel are independent allergen groups with no cross-reactivity to PPD.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis (PASI 22) and psoriatic arthritis has failed methotrexate and cyclosporine. Which biologic agent would be most appropriate for both skin and joint disease?
questions.exp: Secukinumab (anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody) has demonstrated high efficacy for both plaque psoriasis (PASI 90 response) and psoriatic arthritis. IL-17A is a pivotal cytokine in psoriasis pathogenesis. Dupilumab targets the IL-4/IL-13 pathway and is approved for atopic dermatitis. Omalizumab (anti-IgE) is used for chronic spontaneous urticaria. Mepolizumab targets IL-5 in eosinophilic conditions.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man has 7 hypopigmented patches with diminished sensation on the trunk and upper limbs. Slit skin smear shows a bacterial index (BI) of 2+. There is asymmetric nerve thickening. Per the Ridley-Jopling classification, this is most consistent with:
questions.exp: BL leprosy features: more than 5 lesions with partial sensory loss, positive SSS (BI 1-4+), and asymmetric nerve involvement. BT shows 3-5 lesions with definite sensory loss and SSS usually negative. BB shows 'punched-out' appearing lesions. LL is characterized by numerous (>20) symmetrical lesions, diffuse infiltration, high BI (4-6+). WHO classifies >5 lesions or positive SSS as multibacillary.

questions.q: A 75-year-old man presents with tense blisters arising on an urticarial base on the trunk and limbs. Oral mucosa is spared. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The primary target antigen is:
opts: BP180 (NC16A domain of type XVII collagen)
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP), the most common autoimmune bullous disorder in elderly patients, targets the hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (type XVII collagen, especially its NC16A domain) and BP230. Tense blisters arise due to subepidermal splitting. Linear IgG/C3 on DIF at the DEJ is characteristic. Desmoglein antibodies cause pemphigus. Envoplakin is a target in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

questions.q: A 30-year-old sexually active man presents with a painful, soft genital ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and a necrotic base. Inguinal lymph nodes are tender and fluctuant (bubo). The causative organism and treatment of choice are:
opts: Haemophilus ducreyi; Azithromycin 1g single dose orally
Treponema pallidum; Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM
Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3; Doxycycline 100mg BD x 21 days
questions.exp: Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful, soft, non-indurated ulcer with ragged undermined edges, often accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy progressing to fluctuant buboes. Treatment options include: Azithromycin 1g single dose, Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose, or Erythromycin 500mg TDS for 7 days. Fluctuant nodes should be aspirated.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has proximal muscle weakness and symmetric erythematous flat-topped papules over the dorsal MCP and IP joints. She also has a violaceous periorbital rash with edema. Which cutaneous finding is considered PATHOGNOMONIC of dermatomyositis?
opts: Gottron's papules (flat-topped papules over dorsal knuckles)
Shawl sign (erythema over posterior neck and shoulders)
V-sign (erythema on anterior chest and neck)
questions.exp: Gottron's papules — flat-topped, violaceous to erythematous papules and plaques over the dorsal MCP and IP joints — are PATHOGNOMONIC of dermatomyositis. The heliotrope rash is highly characteristic but can rarely occur in other conditions. Shawl sign, V-sign, and periungual changes are highly suggestive but not pathognomonic. Gottron's papules are a major criterion in diagnostic classification.

questions.q: A 5-year-old immunocompetent child presents with multiple pearly white dome-shaped papules with central umbilication on the trunk. The mother reports similar lesions in a classmate. Which statement about this condition is CORRECT?
opts: Caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV-1), a poxvirus; self-limiting in immunocompetent patients
Caused by HPV types 6 and 11; associated with anogenital warts
Associated with primary EBV infection in children
Requires systemic antiviral therapy in all immunocompetent children
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by MCV, a double-stranded DNA poxvirus. MCV-1 is most common in children (spread by skin contact, fomites). MCV-2 is predominant in sexually transmitted adult disease. The condition is self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, typically resolving in 6-18 months. Extensive or persistent disease suggests immunodeficiency (especially HIV).

questions.q: A 65-year-old fair-skinned man presents with a slowly enlarging pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders, visible telangiectasias, and central ulceration on the nasal ala. He has a history of chronic sun exposure. The most likely diagnosis and subtype is:
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype (~60-80%), presenting as a pearly, translucent papule/nodule with rolled ('pearlescent') borders, surface telangiectasias, and central ulceration — classically termed a 'rodent ulcer.' It arises preferentially on the face (nose, inner canthus, periorbital). Morphoeic BCC appears as a flat, indurated, scar-like plaque with indistinct borders, making it more difficult to treat.

questions.q: A patient with severe psoriasis has been on methotrexate 20mg/week for 2 years. Which investigation is MOST important to assess cumulative hepatotoxicity?
opts: Transient elastography (FibroScan) or liver biopsy after 1-1.5g cumulative dose
Annual chest X-ray for pulmonary fibrosis
questions.exp: The most important cumulative toxicity of methotrexate is hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis, which can develop insidiously without elevated LFTs. Transient elastography (FibroScan) is now the preferred non-invasive alternative to liver biopsy, recommended after a cumulative dose of 1-1.5g. Monthly CBC monitors for bone marrow suppression. Pulmonary toxicity monitoring includes DLCO, but cumulative hepatotoxicity is the primary concern.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman develops a rapidly spreading, well-demarcated, bright red, indurated plaque on the right cheek with distinctly elevated advancing margins and high fever following a dental procedure. The most common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Erysipelas is a superficial skin infection involving the dermal lymphatics, caused predominantly by Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes). The characteristic sharp, well-demarcated, raised erythematous margin distinguishes it from cellulitis (poorly defined borders). The face (butterfly distribution) and lower limbs are most commonly affected. Treatment is benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin.

questions.q: Which statement BEST describes the embryological origin and function of melanocytes in the skin?
opts: Neural crest-derived cells that synthesize melanin in melanosomes and transfer them to keratinocytes via dendrites
Bone marrow-derived cells that migrate to the skin and synthesize melanin in lysosomes
Epidermal progenitor cells that differentiate into melanocytes under UV radiation
Dermal fibroblasts that transdifferentiate into melanocytes during skin development
questions.exp: Melanocytes originate from the neural crest and migrate to the skin, uvea, cochlea, and leptomeninges during embryogenesis. In skin, they reside in the basal layer of the epidermis. Melanin is synthesized within melanosomes under enzymatic control (tyrosinase). Melanosomes are transferred to surrounding keratinocytes through long cytoplasmic dendrites. Each melanocyte forms a functional unit with ~36 surrounding keratinocytes ('epidermal melanin unit').

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman is prescribed isotretinoin for severe nodular acne. Which of the following is NOT a recognized side effect of isotretinoin?
questions.exp: Neutropenia is NOT a recognized adverse effect of isotretinoin. Recognized side effects include: mucocutaneous (cheilitis, xerosis, epistaxis, dry eyes), hypertriglyceridemia, elevated liver enzymes, myalgia, photosensitivity, and teratogenicity (absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy — FDA Category X). Pseudotumor cerebri is a rare but serious complication, risk increased if combined with tetracyclines.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic vesicles and papules symmetrically distributed over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. He reports intermittent bloating and diarrhea. Biopsy shows subepidermal vesicle with neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papilla tips. The pathognomonic finding on direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is:
opts: Granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae
Linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction
Intercellular IgG deposits throughout the epidermis
Linear IgA deposits along the basement membrane zone
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). The pathognomonic DIF finding is GRANULAR IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. Linear IgG and C3 at DEJ is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid. Intercellular IgG is seen in pemphigus. Linear IgA characterizes linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Treatment: strict gluten-free diet and dapsone.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with soft, skin-colored, cauliflower-like papillomatous growths on the perianal region. Biopsy confirms condyloma acuminata. Which HPV types are MOST commonly responsible for anogenital warts?
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 (~90%) and 11 (~10%), which have minimal malignant potential. High-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33) are associated with cervical, anal, and penile carcinoma — these cause flat intraepithelial lesions rather than exophytic warts. HPV 1 and 2 cause plantar and common warts. The quadrivalent HPV vaccine covers types 6, 11, 16, 18.

questions.q: A patient is diagnosed with paucibacillary leprosy (2 hypopigmented lesions, sensory impairment, slit skin smear negative). The recommended WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen is:
opts: Rifampicin 600mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months
Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily + Clofazimine 50mg daily for 12 months
Dapsone 100mg daily as monotherapy for 2 years
Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + Clofazimine 50mg daily for 12 months
questions.exp: WHO MDT for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy (1-5 patches): Rifampicin 600mg once monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months. For multibacillary (MB) leprosy (>5 patches or SSS positive): Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + Clofazimine 50mg daily + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months. Monotherapy with dapsone is no longer recommended due to resistance.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman has a well-defined, indurated plaque on the trunk with a lilac (violaceous) border and central ivory-white coloration. She has no Raynaud's phenomenon, no sclerodactyly, and no systemic symptoms. ANA is negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Morphea (localized scleroderma) presents as indurated plaques confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue, with an active 'lilac ring' (violaceous border indicates inflammatory activity) and central ivory-white fibrosis. Unlike systemic sclerosis, morphea lacks Raynaud's phenomenon, acrosclerosis, nailfold capillary changes, and internal organ involvement. Systemic sclerosis-specific antibodies (anti-topoisomerase I, anti-centromere) are absent in morphea.

questions.q: A 70-year-old retired chimney sweep presents with a verrucous, ulcerated nodule on the scrotum. Biopsy confirms well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. This presentation is historically linked to which carcinogen?
opts: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) in coal tar/soot
questions.exp: Scrotal squamous cell carcinoma in chimney sweeps (Pott's cancer, described by Percival Pott in 1775) was the first recognized occupational cancer. It is caused by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) concentrated in chimney soot. This landmark observation established the link between chemical carcinogens and cancer. Arsenic causes arsenical keratoses, Bowen's disease, and SCC on non-sun-exposed areas.

questions.q: A Tzanck smear from the base of a fresh vesicle shows large cells with multiple nuclei, nuclear molding, and margination of chromatin to the periphery. These findings are MOST characteristic of:
questions.exp: Tzanck smear revealing multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) with nuclear molding and peripheral chromatin margination is characteristic of herpesviruses (both HSV-1/2 and VZV). The test cannot distinguish between HSV and VZV — PCR or DIF is required for differentiation. Pemphigus vulgaris shows acantholytic cells (Tzanck cells but mononuclear). Bacterial bullae and inherited EB disorders do not produce multinucleated giant cells.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child has had eczema affecting the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces since age 6 months. Family history reveals asthma and hay fever. Genetic analysis reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene. What does FLG encode and what is its role in skin barrier function?
opts: Filaggrin; aggregates keratin filaments and provides breakdown products that form the natural moisturizing factor (NMF)
Loricrin; major structural protein of the cornified cell envelope
Involucrin; cross-linked substrate of the cornified cell envelope
Claudin-1; component of epidermal tight junctions
questions.exp: FLG encodes filaggrin (filament-aggregating protein), which aggregates keratin intermediate filaments and is then degraded to provide hygroscopic compounds (urocanic acid, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid) that form the natural moisturizing factor (NMF). Loss-of-function FLG mutations are the strongest known genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis, impair skin barrier function, allow allergen penetration, and are associated with the 'atopic march' (eczema to asthma to allergic rhinitis).

questions.q: A family of four presents with intense nocturnal pruritus. The index case is an 8-year-old child with burrows between the fingers and on the wrists. Skin scraping microscopy confirms Sarcoptes scabiei. The recommended treatment approach is:
opts: Permethrin 5% cream applied to entire body below the neck, washed off after 8-14 hours, repeated after 1 week; treat ALL household contacts simultaneously
Benzyl benzoate 25% applied once and washed off after 24 hours; treat only symptomatic members
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg single dose; treat only the index case and symptomatic contacts
Topical sulfur 6% in petrolatum applied only to visible burrows for 3 nights
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies. It must be applied to the entire body surface from the neck down (including scalp and face in infants <2 years), left for 8-14 hours before washing, and repeated after 1 week. CRITICALLY, all household contacts and sexual partners must be treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms to prevent reinfestation. Oral ivermectin is an effective alternative but the treat-all-contacts principle remains essential.
